standard.title: Develop evidence-based conclusions
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4S05 (Conclude from analysis): Students draw basic conclusions from their analysis of information. Students can state what information shows but may not yet explicitly ground conclusions in cited evidence.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop evidence-based conclusions that reflect their inquiry questions, understanding of disciplinary concepts, and evaluation of primary and secondary sources.

nodes.label: What makes a conclusion evidence-based?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between a conclusion based on evidence and a conclusion based on personal preference, limited sources, or unsupported opinion.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what 'evidence-based' means and give an example of an evidence-based conclusion versus one that is not.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the distinction between conclusions based on identified evidence (from valid primary and secondary sources), conclusions based on personal preference, and conclusions based on limited or unreliable sources. Apply these criteria to evaluate examples of student conclusions.
wider: Explore how historians and geographers judge the quality of conclusions in academic writing, and apply these criteria to evaluate the conclusions in a secondary source
Investigate cases where initial evidence suggested one conclusion but additional evidence changed it — discussing what this means for inquiry practice
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't distinguish evidence-based from opinion-based conclusions will conflate personal judgment with analytical finding throughout their HASS work. This conceptual distinction is the prerequisite for all evidence-based reasoning in Year 5 and beyond.

response_modes.reason: Use concrete examples — two conclusions on the same topic, one evidence-based and one opinion-based — and use explicit criteria to identify the difference. The contrast makes the distinction tangible.

success_criteria: Students explain what makes a conclusion 'evidence-based'.
Students identify the difference between at least two contrasting conclusions (one evidence-based, one not).

nodes.label: Identifying valid evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify valid evidence from primary and secondary sources that can be used to form a conclusion, explaining why some evidence is more valid than other evidence for a specific inquiry purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Select two pieces of valid evidence from provided sources and explain why each is relevant to the inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Identify valid evidence from primary and secondary sources (e.g. images, posters, newspaper articles, books, websites) for a HASS inquiry; explain why some sources are more valid than others; consider the reliability, recency and relevance of each source as evidence.
wider: Compare the validity of evidence from a government agency website versus a private blog on the same topic — evaluate the criteria for judging reliability in digital sources
Investigate how the date a secondary source was created affects its validity — exploring how a history textbook written in 1960 may reflect different values from one written in 2020

response_modes.reason: Evidence validity requires applying source evaluation criteria (from AC9HS5S04) in an argument-building context — scaffold the move from 'this source is reliable' to 'this source provides valid evidence for my conclusion because...'

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing digital sources of varying reliability (government agency versus private blog) is an elaboration-supported direction with high practical relevance — this connects to digital literacy and has transferable value beyond HASS.
success_criteria: Students select at least two pieces of valid evidence from sources for an inquiry question.
Students explain why each piece of evidence is relevant and reliable.

nodes.label: Forming conclusions from evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions from identified evidence that consider differing information, reflect disciplinary concepts, and address their inquiry question.
nodes.minimum_width: Write one conclusion grounded in identified evidence that addresses an inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Draw conclusions from primary and secondary sources that: address the inquiry question, reflect understanding of disciplinary concepts (historical, geographic, civic, economic), consider evidence from different sources including those with differing viewpoints, and are clearly distinguished from personal preference.
wider: Draw conclusions about a community or environment (e.g. changing democratic values, patterns of human consumption, environmental change) using evidence from multiple source types
Construct conclusions that explicitly acknowledge uncertainty or conflicting evidence, and explain how this affects confidence in the conclusion

response_modes.reason: Writing evidence-based conclusions is a precision skill — students need practice forming conclusions that make the evidence-to-claim link explicit. Errors (missing citation, over-claiming, under-claiming) need targeted feedback loops.

success_criteria: Students write at least one conclusion that addresses an inquiry question.
Students cite at least two sources as evidence for their conclusion.
Students distinguish their conclusion from personal opinion.

nodes.label: Evaluating the inquiry and conclusions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can consider how the sources they used affected the validity of their conclusions, and identify how additional or different sources would improve the inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Reflect on two sources used in an inquiry and explain how each affected the validity of the conclusions.
nodes.typical_width: Consider the primary and secondary sources used in an inquiry and evaluate how the choice of sources may have influenced the validity and completeness of conclusions; identify what types of sources were missing; explain how including them would improve the investigation.
wider: Evaluate a completed inquiry by assessing whether the conclusions would change if different sources had been used — and identify any gaps or biases introduced by the source selection
Reflect on how the inquiry questions shaped which sources were sought and which perspectives were included or excluded

response_modes.reason: This reflective evaluation node connects source selection, evidence validity and conclusion quality into a metacognitive judgment about the inquiry as a whole. Use structured reflection prompts to scaffold this reflective move.

success_criteria: Students identify how the sources they used affected the validity of their conclusions.
Students suggest at least one way their inquiry could be improved through different or additional sources.
